A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs study SFT versus GRPO for jigsaw learning and knowledge retention in Qwen2.5-VL. Their complete text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original fine-tuning experiments, jigsaw and prior-task benchmark results, perplexity analyses, and learning-rate and restart experiments.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments on 3B and 7B models, benchmark comparisons, and analyses of reasoning data, interference, perplexity, and retention.

M1.justification: The core procedure retains the same jigsaw construction, three reward components, GRPO objective, and SFT on correct RFT-generated rollouts. Periodic optimizer/reference-policy restarts already appear in v1 and remain in v2 Appendix E. GPT-4o reasoning data serve as an added comparator; LBK is an analytical diagnostic.

E1.justification: V2 adds MMMU validation evaluation, extending prior-knowledge coverage to college-level multimodal problems across six disciplines. COCO-derived 3×3 jigsaws and the existing grounding, document/OCR, general VQA, and hallucination benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: V2 adds SFT-Rea-4o-Rollout to Table 1, providing an important reasoning-data comparator. Its high-learning-rate Table 2 replaces the SFT-GT comparator with GPT-4o reasoning-data SFT. SFT-GT and SFT-GRPO-Rollout otherwise match the renamed SFT-Non-Rea and SFT-Rea-GRPO-Rollout methods.

E3.justification: V2 adds Qwen2.5-VL-7B experiments and changes stated SFT defaults from learning rate 1e-6 to 1e-5 and batch size 4 to 16. Table 1 replaces training budgets, including 3B answer-only SFT from 2,738 to 200 steps. New LBK and answer-only perplexity experiments introduce additional measurement protocols and controls.

E4.justification: V2 adds reasoning-versus-nonreasoning interference analysis, answer-only perplexity controls, and reasoning-source Pareto comparisons (Figures 2, 8, and 5). The high-learning-rate analysis is refocused on GPT-4o versus GRPO reasoning data. V1's perplexity-gap distributions and six-epoch rollout analysis are removed; restart analysis and qualitative jigsaw cases are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions show response-distribution boxplots using sampled rollouts. V2 Figure 2 adds shaded bands around LBK curves, but their meaning and calculation are unspecified. Neither PDF identifies training-run counts, seeds, or significance tests, so whether the new shading constitutes additional statistical uncertainty reporting is unresolved.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces v1's 3B answer-only and rollout-SFT jigsaw results of 62% and 66% with 53% and 70% under revised settings. It adds 7B results, including 75% for RFT, GPT-4o comparator results, and MMMU scores. The listed 3B RFT OCRBench score also changes from 77.90 to 77.1. Table 2 and new analytical figures substantially expand the findings.

T1.justification: V2 Section 5.4 adds a Frobenius-norm inequality and the formal LBK definition in Equations 6–7. This extends the existing framework while retaining the one-step decomposition, symmetry theorem, kernel-stability assumption, and appendix proofs, chiefly with updated notation and numbering.

C1.justification: The central data-distribution thesis remains, but v2 adds interference magnitude and direction, and the protective role of reasoning trajectories, as explicit main contributions. It also narrows the rollout-SFT claim from avoiding or overcoming catastrophic forgetting to reducing it in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.

C2.justification: V2 explains reasoning as connecting novel answers to existing perceptual abilities and reducing interference magnitude. It further argues that perplexity explains why GRPO data preserve knowledge better even when GPT-4o data have smaller LBK. V1's probability-normalization explanation of residual forgetting is dropped. Limitations now cover 3B/7B, and model-selection discussion adds InternVL memory constraints.

D1.justification: V2 supplies the GPT-4o generation prompt and example response, plus the empty-thinking-tag control for answer-only perplexity. Hardware reporting changes from two to four A800 GPUs, while the explicit GRPO gradient-accumulation count is omitted. A new reproducibility statement promises future open-source code without supplying an access link.

R1.justification: V2 adds Lai et al. on forgetting and RL's Razor, positioning its data-based explanation alongside the latter's KL-minimality account. MMMU and InternVL references are added, while several overview citations, including Jigsaw Clustering, PODNet, and VideoChat-R1, are removed. The principal positioning relative to GRPO and learning dynamics remains.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and contribution narrative are substantially reframed. Related work is compressed from numbered subsections into thematic paragraphs, and Sections 5.4–5.6 are reordered and rewritten. Limitations move to Appendix B, and ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-usage statements are added.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with three training-data paths, Table 1 gains separate 3B/7B blocks, and Table 2 is expanded. New LBK, perplexity, Pareto, and prompt displays replace several earlier plots. The original jigsaw examples and restart plots are retained but relocated to the appendix.

improvement.justification: V1's comparison confounds data source with the presence of reasoning. V2 substantially addresses this through GPT-4o reasoning controls: at 70% 3B jigsaw accuracy, GRPO-rollout SFT retains 84.6 RefCOCO accuracy versus 74.2 for GPT-4o-rollout SFT (Table 1). The 7B experiments and more qualified forgetting claims further strengthen the empirical case. Although the kernel-bound interpretation remains indirect and uncertainty bands are undefined, the improved controls provide substantially stronger support for the central data-distribution explanation.
